castigate

KAS-ti-gate · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To castigate is to criticize or reprimand someone severely, especially in public.

The senator was castigated by the press for the leaked memo.

Example

The newspaper's editorial castigated the mayor for months of broken promises, calling the administration a complete failure.

A harsh, public, formal condemnation in print is exactly the severe criticism castigate describes.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

condemn: To condemn is to pass judgment that something is wrong -- a court, a council, or a newspaper can condemn an act in one formal verdict and move on. To castigate is hotter and more personal: severe, detailed criticism heaped on the offender.

denounce: To denounce is to accuse in public -- to stand up and inform the world of a wrongdoing and who did it, often revealing it for the first time. To castigate assumes the wrong is already known and punishes it with words: severe, stinging criticism of the offender.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

praise: express approval

commend: express formal approval

Where it sits · how harsh and public the condemnation

criticize → castigate → excoriate

criticize vs. castigate: To criticize is a general, everyday act of pointing out faults; to castigate is a much harsher, often public condemnation.

excoriate vs. castigate: Excoriate goes even further than castigate, implying an almost scathing, merciless verbal attack.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cast: pure (Latin (castus))

suffix — -igate: to make, to do (Latin (agere))

Put it together: cast ('pure', from Latin castus) + -igate ('to make, to do') together trace back to the idea of correcting someone to make them 'pure' again -- the harsh, formal criticism castigate now describes.

Use the root in a new word: chaste: Chaste comes from the same Latin root castus ('pure'), the same root buried inside castigate.

Strength Check

Word Choice
